summary: Picture one astronaut, three months out from Earth, when the Sun throws off a major flare. A message home can take more than 20 minutes each way, so nobody on the ground can make the call in time. We built Vigil for that moment. It is an offline crew health monitor that watches the cabin radiation sensors and the solar event records, and it answers one of the first questions that the crew will have to ask: "What is my radiation risk now, and what do I do?" Vigil shows one level and one action, and when a Warning pops up, one tap opens the shelter checklist. Our demo replays the real March 2012 storm that NASA's MSL RAD detector measured on its way to Mars. We tested the shelter rule on the 7 storms RAD measured, then on 40 years of GOES proton data, the full RAD record and 17 years of LRO CRaTER data, where it sent the crew to shelter in all 83 measured events. Every number in the app links to its source, and anything simulated is specifically marked. A large storm can deliver hundreds of mSv in a day, and the crew needs a clear call before the peak.
details:
What it does

Vigil is a crew health monitor for a single astronaut on a 180-day trip to Mars. Its main job is radiation. When the Sun erupts, protons can reach the ship within hours, and Earth is too far away to make the call in time. Vigil watches the cabin dose rate and the solar event records and tells the crew how big the risk is and what to do next. It also keeps track of cabin air and body systems, so the crew sees their health in one place.

How it works

  • There are four alert levels. A big flare or a fast CME raises a Caution before the protons arrive. If only one sensor spikes, Vigil shows Verify and asks the crew to check it, so a bad sensor can't send anyone to the shelter. When the dose rate stays above twice the baseline on two or more sensors for 30 minutes, it's a Warning.
  • From a Warning, one tap opens shelter procedure SH-1. The crew ticks off each step while a timer runs.
  • After the peak, Vigil estimates when the storm will clear and shows a 90% range. Once every sensor stays below 1.5 times the baseline for an hour, the Warning drops to Caution and the crew can leave.
  • A dose budget tracks the storm dose against the NASA-STD-3001 limits: 250 mSv for one solar event and 600 mSv for a career.
  • The crew can do a 30-second health check by voice or by tap. The note reader picks out symptoms such as "head feels full" and suggests them, and the crew decides what to mark.
  • Ask AI answers questions from the live alerts and the log. It works offline, shows where each answer came from, and has no way to change an alert. It won't diagnose or suggest treatment. It sends the crew to the flight surgeon for that.
  • A delay switch simulates the light-time to Earth and full blackouts. When the link comes back, the ground gets a summary.
  • The other views cover cabin radiation, space weather, cabin air, body systems, a daily report you can save as PDF or JSON, a flight-surgeon handoff, and a limits explorer for what-if values.

Data and testing

  • The replay uses measured MSL RAD dose rates from the 2012 cruise to Mars, plus the real flare, CME and proton records from 5 to 7 March 2012. The crew, the sensor spread, the cabin air and the vitals are simulated, and a striped Simulation band says so on every screen.
  • We tested four shelter rules on the 7 solar storms that RAD measured in 541 days of data. Our rule got the crew into the shelter before the peak in 6 of the 7, with no false entries, and avoided 64% of the storm dose. The one late entry was a slow, low event on 13 March 2012. Its peak came in the first reading, and the rule waited 30 minutes to confirm.
  • Then we went bigger: 40 years of GOES proton data (1986 to 2026), the full MSL RAD record (466,657 observations) and 17 years of LRO CRaTER data, with 2020 to 2026 held back as a test. The entry rule sent the crew to shelter in 83 of 83 measured events. On 34 new shelter stays, the clear-time range held the real clear time in 89.8% of the hourly checks.
  • Unit tests cover the rules engine, the forecast and the assistant. End-to-end and accessibility tests (Playwright and axe, WCAG 2.1 AA) run on a desktop and a phone screen.

Why it matters

  • In a storm, the crew gets one clear action within seconds, with no wait for Earth.
  • False alarms are rare, so the crew keeps trusting the alarm and keeps working when nothing is wrong.
  • Every number links to a NASA standard, a paper or a data set, so a flight surgeon can check the reasoning.
  • All the thresholds live in one JSON file, so a scientist can change a limit without touching code.
  • The same approach would carry over to lunar missions and Mars surface habitats.

Tools and languages

Vigil is a static web app written in TypeScript with React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4, shadcn/ui on Radix, Motion, Recharts and three.js. vite-plugin-pwa lets it run offline after the first load. Vitest, Playwright, axe and ESLint handle testing. The data study is in Python (NumPy, Numba, pandas, SciPy, scikit-learn, netCDF4, Matplotlib). Voice input uses the browser's Web Speech API. Ask AI can optionally use Llama 3.2 running in the browser through WebLLM, Claude with your own key, or any OpenAI-compatible API. It needs no special hardware and runs in a browser on a laptop, tablet or phone.

What makes it creative

  • You watch the alarm work on a real storm, measured by a real detector on its way to Mars.
  • The Verify level means one faulty sensor can't trigger a shelter entry.
  • Our clear-time range was tested on events it had never seen, and we show the 90% figure from that test.
  • The assistant can read everything but can't act. It can't acknowledge, suppress or change an alert.

What we thought about

  • A dim cabin and gloved hands: big touch targets (48 px for crew actions), red only for Warning and amber only for Caution, and every color paired with an icon and a word.
  • Safety: nobody can suppress a Warning, and two sensors at 10 times the baseline for 5 minutes always raise one.
  • Privacy: the crew member decides who sees each health entry.
  • Honest data: Simulation mode (violet, with stripes) and Real-world data mode (teal) look different on every screen, and measured values, simulated values and team assumptions all carry labels. Vigil is not for clinical use.
  • No network: it keeps working after the first load.
